**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Enforce auth by default on processing trigger**

`triggerProcessing` uses `if (!principal && auth.required)` so an unset `auth.required` (the default config) allows unauthenticated callers to enqueue processing jobs. Other routes in this package treat `undefined` as auth-required (`auth.required !== false`), so this creates an inconsistent and exposed path that can be abused for unsolicited background work.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Check file authorization before enqueuing processing**

This endpoint forwards `fileId` and client-supplied processing inputs directly to `service.triggerProcessing` without any ownership/readability check for that file. Because processing writes/updates artifacts keyed by `fileId`/`versionId`, a caller can trigger work for files they should not control, which risks unauthorized artifact mutation and avoidable compute load.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Default processing version to a real version identifier**

When the request omits `versionId`, the route falls back to `fileId` (`versionId: body.versionId || fileId`). `fileId` and `versionId` are different identifiers, so this stores artifacts under a non-existent/wrong version key and those artifacts will not match normal version-based retrieval paths.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**Weak djb2 hash breaks the idempotency conflict guarantee** `hashPayload` uses a non-cryptographic 32-bit djb2 hash to detect when an idempotency key is reused with a different payload. The 32-bit output space (~4 billion values) is small enough that collisions are plausible — for adversarial inputs they can be crafted deliberately. When two different payloads collide to the same hash, the check `existing.idempotencyPayloadHash !== expectedHash` evaluates to `false`, so the `idempotencyConflict()` error is **never thrown** and the second (conflicting) request silently replays the first session. This directly violates the idempotency contract. Every other sensitive hash in this codebase (`hashUploadSessionToken`, `hashToken`) correctly uses SHA-256. Use the same approach here: ```typescript import { createHash } from 'crypto'; function hashPayload(input: CreateSessionInput, ctx: { principalId?: string; tenantId?: string }): string { const payload = { p: input.policy, fn: input.fileName, s: input.size, mt: input.mimeType, fid: input.fileId, md: input.metadata, pr: ctx.principalId, tn: ctx.tenantId, }; return createHash('sha256').update(JSON.stringify(payload)).digest('hex'); } ```

Path: filefn/server/src/upload-sessions/service.ts Line: 93-112 Comment: **Weak djb2 hash breaks the idempotency conflict guarantee** `hashPayload` uses a non-cryptographic 32-bit djb2 hash to detect when an idempotency key is reused with a different payload. The 32-bit output space (~4 billion values) is small enough that collisions are plausible — for adversarial inputs they can be crafted deliberately. When two different payloads collide to the same hash, the check `existing.idempotencyPayloadHash !== expectedHash` evaluates to `false`, so the `idempotencyConflict()` error is **never thrown** and the second (conflicting) request silently replays the first session. This directly violates the idempotency contract. Every other sensitive hash in this codebase (`hashUploadSessionToken`, `hashToken`) correctly uses SHA-256. Use the same approach here: ```typescript import { createHash } from 'crypto'; function hashPayload(input: CreateSessionInput, ctx: { principalId?: string; tenantId?: string }): string { const payload = { p: input.policy, fn: input.fileName, s: input.size, mt: input.mimeType, fid: input.fileId, md: input.metadata, pr: ctx.principalId, tn: ctx.tenantId, }; return createHash('sha256').update(JSON.stringify(payload)).digest('hex'); } ``` How can I resolve this? If you propose a fix, please make it concise. `````

**Inconsistent tie-breaking comparison between sort and cursor filter** `fileSortComparator` breaks ties using `localeCompare` (locale-aware string comparison), while `isAfterCursor` uses the `>` operator (lexicographic code-point comparison). These two comparisons can produce different orderings for mixed-case IDs or IDs containing special characters, causing cursor pagination to skip or duplicate items.

P2: `computeAndCheckDuplicate` and `verifyHash` reference sibling methods via `this`, but the returned value is a plain object literal. If any consumer destructures these methods (e.g., `const { computeAndCheckDuplicate } = service`), `this` will be `undefined` and the call will throw. Prefer capturing the object in a variable and using direct references, or bind the methods explicitly.
